target: AG1's opening claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves daily life, work, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI is not good for society in practice because its deployment tends to create recurring harms that undermine social well-being: it can displace workers and concentrate power, weaken students’ critical thinking by encouraging dependence on AI-generated answers, reproduce and amplify racial bias, and create serious privacy risks through large-scale data collection and surveillance.

target: AG2's assumption that AI deployment in practice inevitably produces major recurring harms that cannot be prevented or counterbalanced.
objection: Those harms are not unavoidable or inevitably dominant; with governance and design choices such as reskilling, scaffolded educational uses, fairness-aware training, auditing, and privacy-preserving techniques, AI’s negative effects can be reduced enough that the harms need not recur at the scale assumed.

target: AG1's claim that AI improves safety, health, and accessibility enough to make it broadly beneficial.
objection: AI's visible benefits come with predictable harms: safety monitoring can fail in novel or edge cases, medical decision support can mislead clinicians or patients and worsen health outcomes, and accessibility tools can require sensitive data collection that increases privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG2's claim that AI hazard monitoring is not dependable and cannot reliably prevent accidents.
objection: That assumption is false in general: AI safety systems can be designed and validated to detect hazards earlier than humans, predict failures before they occur, and use reliability safeguards such as calibration, continuous monitoring, and human escalation, so they can reliably improve workplace safety.

target: AG1's claim that AI will improve information reliability by enabling detection, provenance, and fact-checking.
objection: Widespread AI use tends to increase misinformation and manipulation because generative AI makes fake text, images, and audio cheap to produce, and AI-driven ranking systems often amplify sensational content; that makes it harder for people to distinguish truth from fabrication and undermines social coordination.

target: AG2's assumption that cheaper AI-generated falsehoods will, overall, produce greater information unreliability because verification cannot keep pace.
objection: That is not warranted because AI can also be used for verification at scale through deepfake detection, provenance/authentication, watermarking, and assisted fact-checking, which can improve information reliability rather than degrade it.

target: AG1's claim that AI workplace safety monitoring reliably reduces accidents.
objection: AI monitoring can undermine the practical behavior that creates safety by producing automation bias: people trust the system too much, pay less attention to weak signals, reduce reporting and vigilance, and miss failures when the model is wrong.

target: AG2's claim that automation bias makes AI hazard monitoring unreliable.
objection: Automation bias is not inevitable; in safety-critical settings AI can be deployed with human-in-the-loop procedures, alarm management, explicit independent checks, training, and auditing so that AI improves hazard detection while humans retain meaningful vigilance.

target: AG1's assumption that organizations will maintain effective safeguards when AI is deployed at scale.
objection: That assumption is false because firms face strong incentives to cut verification and auditing costs; safety harms are often delayed or hard to attribute, while throughput pressures are immediate, so oversight tends to degrade into box-ticking and the supposed safeguards often do not persist in practice.

target: AG2's claim that even if safety monitoring is unreliable in some deployments, the harms outweigh AI's broader benefits.
objection: Even if some workplaces cut corners, that does not show AI is not good overall; AI also provides broad, scalable benefits in convenience, health, learning, productivity, and accessibility that can offset limitations in one safety route.

target: AG1's balancing claim that AI's convenience, productivity, and accessibility benefits can offset safety-monitoring shortcomings.
objection: That offset assumption fails because safety-critical errors can be catastrophic and irreversible, so even relatively low-frequency failures can outweigh incremental gains; moreover, the same cost pressures that erode safety safeguards can also degrade the quality of AI in health and other high-stakes uses.

target: AG2's narrow safety critique focused on workplace hazard monitoring.
objection: That attack is too narrow because AI can improve safety in broader everyday ways too, such as helping with navigation and scheduling to reduce risky mistakes and supporting health-related decisions that can prevent harm; those benefits do not depend on workplace monitoring.

target: AG1's broader claim that AI is good despite harms because it improves convenience, productivity, and accessibility.
objection: AI is not good for society because mainstream deployment replaces human judgment with opaque predictions that people cannot meaningfully evaluate or challenge, which undermines autonomy and critical thinking.

target: AG2's claim that opacity in AI necessarily causes lost autonomy and critical thinking.
objection: AI can be deployed with explanations, uncertainty cues, user override, and co-pilot/tutor-style interactions so that users can evaluate and steer recommendations rather than passively accept them; in such designs, AI can augment judgment instead of replacing it.

target: AG1's claim that mainstream AI is contestable through explanations and user control.
objection: Those protections are usually not meaningful in practice because explanations are often superficial or post-hoc, override is constrained by workflow integration, and companies optimize for speed and engagement rather than genuine contestability.

target: AG1's claim that users can meaningfully contest AI recommendations in mainstream systems.
objection: Mainstream AI is often embedded in background ranking, eligibility, and scoring systems, so users cannot inspect or challenge the inference when it matters; even when reasons are shown, they are often generic or incomplete, and practical power to appeal is limited.

target: AG1's claim that AI-guided decisions can preserve autonomy through simple override options and explanations.
objection: Superficial overrides and explanations do not create real contestability because the AI is still the default path and the reasons shown are rarely decision-grade, so users are nudged toward reliance rather than independent judgment.

target: AG2's assumption that mainstream AI use generally erodes critical thinking and autonomy.
objection: In many everyday contexts, especially education and professional work, AI is used as assistance that removes time-consuming steps and lets users spend more time on higher-value reasoning, revision, and creativity, which can strengthen critical thinking rather than weaken it.

target: AG1's claim that mainstream AI mostly supports reasoning rather than substituting for it.
objection: That assumption often fails because many popular tools are answer generators that produce near-finished drafts or recommendations people can simply copy or submit, so the user can end up selecting AI-produced content instead of constructing the reasoning themselves.

target: AG2's claim that opacity and AI assistance generally undermine autonomy and critical thinking.
objection: In typical assistive use, users actively evaluate and revise drafts against external criteria like facts, rubrics, domain rules, or source checks, so opacity does not automatically erase judgment or make errors sticky.

target: AG1's assumption that users routinely verify AI outputs with external checks in ordinary use.
objection: That assumption is usually false because time pressure, skill gaps, and workflow integration mean many users do not deeply verify outputs, so drafts and summaries get copied or used downstream and errors propagate.

target: AG2's view that opacity necessarily destroys autonomy and informed consent.
objection: Autonomy can be preserved through recourse, appeals, human decision-makers, and institutional review rather than direct inspection of model internals; if accountable organizations can correct decisions through established channels, opacity alone does not cause lost autonomy.

target: AG1's claim that appeals and oversight can preserve autonomy and informed choice in AI-mediated decisions.
objection: Appeals and oversight often fail to restore autonomy because they do not provide decision-grade reasons, depend on the same opaque system, and impose time and power barriers that make recourse ineffective for ordinary users.

target: AG2's assumption that institutions cannot supply inspectable criteria and evidence for meaningful oversight.
objection: That assumption is too strong: AI decision pipelines can be made auditable by logging inputs, sources, and policy steps, retrieval-based systems can tie outputs to checkable evidence, and audits can be conducted through contracts or privacy-preserving methods.

target: AG1's claim that audit trails and reviewable criteria make contestation meaningful.
objection: That picture is often insufficient because many AI outputs rest on latent features and opaque statistical correlations that do not map cleanly onto contestable criteria, so even audits and recorded inputs may not reveal whether the decision truly satisfied the stated policy.

target: AG2's claim that meaningful oversight is structurally blocked by proprietary secrecy and privacy limits.
objection: Those limits do not make faithful review impossible in general because deployments can log inputs, cite sources, allow third-party audits, and use secure or contractual access arrangements so reviewers can still test compliance with the stated criteria.

target: AG1's claim that later appeals and correction mechanisms preserve autonomy despite opaque AI guidance.
objection: That is too late to solve the problem because autonomy and informed consent depend on contestation at the moment guidance changes behavior, while AI often creates irreversible downstream commitments and sticky errors before any review can occur.
